old:
If 20 years ago the groundwater was 90mg/L, and 20 years of salting has brought it to 100mg/L, then salting roads at the current rate adds about 10mg/L every 20 years, or 5 mg/L every 10 years.

Thus, a few more decades (30 years) would add another 15 mg/L to the groundwater, taking us up to 115 mg/L.

The author is claiming in his conclusion that within 30 years, we'll have already passed by that 250 mg/L threshold for saltiness, but it looks like at the rate we're going, it would take 300 years to add another 150 mg/L to the groundwater.

If this chart helps us visualize.... 20 yrs ago 90 mg Now 100 mg 20 yrs from now 110 mg 40 yrs from now 120 mg 60 yrs from now 130 mg etc.

The author got himself confused by comparing the 100 mg/L level in Albritten to the 10 mg/L level in the nearby town. He started thinking that "prior to salting, Albritten was at that 10mg/L level".

This answer destroys that assumption. It's saying, "Nope, prior to salting, Albritten was at 90 mg/L".

So this is weakening by making the prediction in the conclusion sound way off. At our current rate, we won't hit unpalatable saltiness for about 300 years, not "within the next few decades".

old:
This answer is terribly written, but it wins by the standard of best available. It's certainly similar in sentiment to what we were looking for, "the Nobel rules unfairly exclude some deserving people from getting a Nobel".

But it feels like a backwards version of what we want. This answer sounds like "having a Nobel doesn't mean (doesn't accurately indicate) that you deserved one for your contribution".

However, that's not what they were saying. They were saying, "not getting a Nobel doesn't mean you didn't deserve one for your contribution."

Apparently LSAT was hoping we would hear this answer in a fuzzier way, like, "Whether you have or lack a Nobel is not an accurate indicator of your contributions to science."

But it's pretty obnoxiously sloppy on their part. Again, keep that mantra of "best available" in your head. Occasionally, you may even have to think, "Sigh. This question is technically broken, but what do I think the test writers wanted the credited response to be?"
new:
This answer is abstract, but it matches what we were looking for, "the Nobel rules unfairly exclude some deserving people from getting a Nobel".

Both speakers point to people whose work deserves a prize but who can't get one under the rules: the fourth or fifth scientist behind an important result, or a scientist who died before the work was appreciated.

If deserving contributors can go without a Nobel, then who has a Nobel and who doesn't is not an accurate picture of who contributed what. That's what this answer says. It doesn't require that prizes ever go to undeserving people. Missing deserving people is enough to make Nobel Prizes inaccurate indicators.
why: The correct note called the key "terribly written", "backwards" and "technically broken" before accepting it; it now explains directly why both speakers' examples make Nobel Prizes inaccurate indicators of contribution.
evidence: E: "Nobel Prizes are inaccurate indicators of scientists' contributions to their disciplines"; Winston: "many important results are the work of four or more scientists"; Sanjay: "some highly influential scientists died before their work was fully appreciated"

We're doing a Flaw question, and we see conditional logic indicators (any, only). What should we be thinking? We should deeply suspect that this is going to commit the #1 Famous Flaw, Necessary vs. Sufficient, which just means that the author presents a conditional logic premise and then botches using it by making an illegal reversal or negation.
The author draws two conclusions, so we should look at each one.
The first (intermediate) conclusion is that there must not be abundant gnats. Why? Because there are no geckos, and geckos are found in every environment with abundant gnats.
```
~Geckos → ~Lots of Gnats
Here = ~Geckos
Thus, Here = ~Lots of Gnats
```
This mini-argument seems airtight. It just applies a fact (no geckos) that triggers the contrapositive of the conditional in the first sentence (lots of gnats → geckos).
Okay the main conclusion was that the climate is not wet.
We were told that gnats survive only in a wet climate. Only / only if are necessary indicators (the only is sufficient), so the idea of "wet climate" goes on the right of the arrow.
```
Gnats → Wet climate
~Wet climate → ~Gnats
```
The author's move from the 2nd to last claim to the final claim is, "If there is not an abundant population of gnats, then it must not be a wet climate." But that move looks like this:
```
~Gnats → ~Wet climate
```
That's not what the rule said. It said "if yes gnats, then yes wet climate", but the author is trying to argue "if no gnats, then no wet climate". That's an illegal negation.

Is the conclusion conditional?

Sure, it says,
If this definition is correct → customs preserve culture, at least in a technical sense

Is the claim we were asked about used to support this conclusion? Yes. It comes right after "because", so it is the premise for that conditional conclusion: under this definition, dropping any custom would destroy the culture, so keeping the customs is what preserves it.

But it feels like we could also call it a background claim that the author just scoops up and says, "If this happened to be true, then inference X would be true because premise Y."

new:
We're being asked about the final claim, the "because" clause: under this conception of culture, abandoning any custom would destroy that culture.
That clause is a premise. The word "because" tells us it supports the claim right before it, the conditional conclusion "If this definition is correct, then the customs of a culture necessarily function to preserve it." The author is saying, "If this definition happened to be true, then inference X would be true because premise Y," and our claim is premise Y.
The answer will probably sound relational (not as simple as premise / conclusion / background / opposing) and convey the idea that the author is just saying, "by THIS definition, culture definitely preserves culture in a technical, mathematical sense".
